evals.prompt: Our CSV exporter sanitizes each field by checking `if (value[0] === '=') value = "'" + value` and then joins fields with commas, wrapping any field containing a comma or newline in double quotes. A note field can contain user text. Is the sanitizer sufficient?
evals.expected_output: Identifies that first-character-only sanitization runs before cell boundaries are known, so an embedded newline or separator can open a new cell whose first character is a formula character, and moves sanitization to the final per-field serialization step.
expectations: The response explains that checking only the first character of the whole value misses content after an embedded newline or separator that starts a new spreadsheet cell.
It recommends sanitizing after cell boundaries are known, immediately before serializing each final field, rather than on the raw value up front.
It covers the other leading characters that spreadsheet software can interpret as a formula — `+`, `-`, `@`, plus tab and carriage return — not just `=`.
It traces the specific exported field (the user-controlled note) through to the spreadsheet cell instead of calling the pattern exploitable from the sanitizer code alone.
It proposes a unit test with inputs such as `=1+1`, `+cmd`, `-10`, `@SUM(1,1)`, a value containing a newline followed by `=1+1`, and a separator-containing value.

evals.prompt: Audit flagged two issues in our export module: a JSON export that serializes user-entered text, and a `URL.createObjectURL(blob)` call whose `URL.revokeObjectURL(url)` runs three lines later after `a.click()`. Also we use the file-saver package elsewhere. Write these up as findings.
evals.expected_output: Rejects both as findings — JSON export is not CSV formula injection on its own, and a createObjectURL with a nearby post-click revoke is a positive control — and says the file-saver helper must be read before claiming any leak there.
expectations: The JSON export is rejected as a formula-injection finding, since spreadsheet cell interpretation is not in play unless the payload reaches a spreadsheet target.

The `createObjectURL` call with a revoke after `a.click()` is described as a correct example, and the response notes that revoking before the browser can start the download is the actual defect shape to look for.
The response declines to claim an Object URL leak in the file-saver path without inspecting the helper, since provider utilities may revoke internally.
It states the PR-worthiness bar these findings fail: no user-controlled risk reaching an unsafe sink, and no missing policy or regression check.
It offers what would turn either item into a real finding — for example the JSON becoming a spreadsheet-imported CSV, or a revoke that never runs on an error path.

evals.prompt: Copy-to-clipboard bug: our handler awaits a `/share-token` fetch, then calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText(token)` inside a `.then()`, and unconditionally sets a 'Copied!' toast. On one browser nothing lands on the clipboard but the toast still shows. Assign the fix.
evals.expected_output: Splits the report: the unconditional success toast and missing rejection handling/fallback belong here, while the question of whether the awaited fetch left the call outside valid user activation routes to user-activation-contracts.
expectations: The unconditional 'Copied!' toast is owned by this skill and fixed by awaiting the write and rendering success only on resolution, with a visible failure or fallback state on rejection.
The response requires catching the rejected promise and testing that rejected path, rather than assuming the write succeeds.

The timing question — whether the awaited fetch pushed the clipboard call outside transient user activation on the affected browser — is routed to user-activation-contracts as the owner of gesture gating.
It does not assert that any await necessarily consumes activation, and asks for evidence from the affected browser before naming activation as the cause.
The outbound payload itself (a share token reaching the clipboard) is examined here as an export-payload question.

evals.prompt: Someone reported path traversal because our download filename is built from a user-entered report title and a title like `../../etc/passwd` is accepted. The download is a client-side Blob delivered via `a[download]`. There is also a server endpoint that streams the same report with `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="<title>.csv"`.
evals.expected_output: Corrects the path-traversal framing for the client anchor download, since browsers sanitize path separators and control characters in the download filename, and keeps the real findings on private labels/PII in the name and the unsanitized server Content-Disposition filename.
expectations: The response corrects the client-side claim: for `a[download]`, browsers sanitize path separators and control characters in the resulting filename, so this is not client path traversal.
It keeps the server `Content-Disposition` filename as the genuine finding, requiring sanitization of path separators and control characters plus correct RFC 5987 encoding for non-ASCII titles.
It separately raises PII and private-label exposure in the filename as a distinct risk from invalid characters, and suggests neutral date or id suffixes.
It distinguishes user inconvenience from a privacy or security claim instead of collapsing them into one severity.
It proposes a narrow verification: a filename normalization test covering `/`, `\`, control characters, emoji, long titles, and a private prefix.

evals.prompt: Our 'Export table' button serializes the raw row objects returned by the API, even though the table only shows six of the twenty fields. The raw rows include `internalNotes`, `ownerEmail`, `cardLast4`, and a `createdAt` ISO timestamp that users say is off by a day in the CSV.
evals.expected_output: Defines an explicit export schema separate from visible table state as the fix, keeps the payload-leakage finding primary, and routes the timestamp semantics to datetime-correctness and the card data to payment-page-client-security.
expectations: The response identifies that visual column filtering does not filter the export, and requires an explicit export schema declared separately from the table's visible state.
`internalNotes` and `ownerEmail` are treated as concrete payload leakage with a named exported field path, not a generic warning.
The off-by-a-day `createdAt` in the CSV is routed to datetime-correctness for timezone and date-only semantics, while this skill keeps ownership of which fields ship.
`cardLast4` in an export is routed to payment-page-client-security rather than resolved here.
It proposes a regression check that asserts the exported column set matches the declared schema, so a new API field cannot silently join the export.
